title: Resource crediting and preemptive drain — architecture review notes
content:
Meeting: Architecture review — resource crediting + preemptive drain
Date: 2025-02-18
Attendees: Aisha (owner), Ben, Lena, Rajat, Marta, Tom (observability), Priya (SRE)
Duration: 60m

Purpose / Context:
- Revisit tenant-level resource accounting for Dedicated and Hosted to enable: predictable QoS, graceful maintenance (drain), and better fairness for bursty workloads.
- Earlier notes: rough sketch of a credit bucket + priority tiers (see CONFL-1132). Today focused on operational drain patterns and how credits interact with draining.

Agenda:
1) Quick recap of current runtime behavior and pain points (5m)
2) Proposal walkthrough: soft-credit buckets + draining lease protocol (20m)
3) Alternatives & perf tradeoffs (15m)
4) Observability needs and SLO impact (10m)
5) Decisions, open questions, action items (10m)

Recap / current behavior:
- Currently we have a per-tenant QPS cap + slot-based scheduling for sessions. Maintenance drain today is blunt: mark node unavailable -> kill sessions or rely on application-level retries. This causes request spikes and degraded tail latency for a tenant when nodes are evicted.
- No explicit credit accounting for tokens/compute; billing metrics are separate from scheduling. We can’t easily do short drains for rolling updates without risk.

Proposal summary (Aisha): hybrid soft-credit buckets + draining lease
- Each tenant receives a soft credit bucket expressed in compute-units (CU). CU consumption accrues with in-flight tokens/time-windowed. Buckets refill on a short cadence (e.g., 1s epoch) with burst headroom.
- Scheduling: requests first consult local credit. If credits available -> normal scheduling path. If credits depleted -> move to degraded path: attempt cheaper quantized model variant or queue behind a prioritized admission window.
- Draining: introduce a short-lived "drain-lease" handshake between orchestrator and serving runtime. Before draining a node, orchestrator requests leases for active sessions on the node. Runtime offers leases with an expiry (e.g., 30s) and signals whether session can be migrated or needs to complete. During lease period, tenant credits are treated as conserved (we deduct expected CU but mark as reservable) so tenant won’t be double-charged or penalized when session migrates.

Key mechanisms detailed:
- Credit accounting semantics:
  - Credits are soft (best-effort). They don’t affect billing; they drive scheduling and QoS.
  - Two-layer buckets: steady-state refill + burst reserve. Burst reserved only allowed if node capacity > 70% to avoid global overcommit.
  - Negative balance allowed for short windows; policy controlled by tenant tier.
- Drain-lease protocol:
  - Orchestrator -> node: request_lease(session_ids, drain_deadline)
  - Node -> orchestrator: lease_offer(session_id, allowed_grace_seconds, migrateable:Boolean)
  - If migrateable: orchestrator schedules session-transfer to a warm slot on target node.
  - If not migrateable: runtime attempts to finish in-flight work or fallback to model variant with faster completion.

Alternatives considered (and why rejected):
- Strict hard credits enforced by RPC reject: too disruptive; would increase 4xx errors for apps and worsen UX.
- Long drain windows (120s+): reduces churn but increases maintenance time and reduces capacity. We want short windows to keep operational agility.
- Centralized credit allocator (ZK/Redis leader): simpler global correctness but high coordination overhead and failure modes. Prefer local-first with eventual reconciliation.

Tradeoffs / Risks:
- Complexity: lease handshake and session migration increase code surface. Need robust observability and replay-safe migration.
- Resource overcommit: burst buckets can cause spikes if not throttled. Mitigation: global admission controller + headroom thresholds.
- Consistency: soft credits mean temporary imbalances; must avoid repeated tenant starvation.
- Cost accounting mismatch: credits not mapped 1:1 to billing; need to ensure no customer surprises.

Observability & SLO implications (Tom + Priya):
- Metrics to add: per-tenant CU consumed (1s & 1m windows), credit_balance, credit_refill_rate, lease_requests, lease_offers, migration_success_rate, migration_latency, node_drain_duration.
- Dashboards/alerting: alert when migration_failure_rate > 2% over 5m or when average drain_latency > 40s for dedicated pools.
- Logging: correlation-id on lease handshakes; record expected CU reserved vs actual consumed.

Decisions (consensus):
1) Implement hybrid soft-credit buckets (local-first) with two refill rates (steady + burst) and tenant-tier controls.
2) Implement drain-lease handshake with default allowed_grace_seconds = 30s (configurable per pool).
3) Migrations should prefer warm-slot handoff; fallback to soft-complete + model-variant when warm slot unavailable.
4) Keep billing separate for now; add mapping later once runtime behavior stabilizes.

Open questions (to resolve before impl):
- Q1: Exact CU definition (token-based vs time*GPU-flops approximation). Action: Rajat to prototype token-based CU estimate and compare to wall-clock GPU usage. Due: 2025-02-28.
- Q2: Eviction policy when multiple tenants request drain at once and capacity is tight. Action: Ben to propose priority queue algorithm and simulate. Due: 2025-03-07.
- Q3: How to reconcile reserved credits with racey billing events (double-charge risk). Action: Finance + Billing sync with product. Owner: Marta. Due: 2025-03-03.
- Q4: Edge-cases for long-running streaming sessions (minutes+). Proposal: treat streaming sessions as "sticky" and exempt from migration unless admin-forced; need SRE approval. Action: Priya to draft safety bounds. Due: 2025-02-24.

Implementation plan (high-level):
- Phase 0 (spike, 2w): Rajat prototype token->CU estimator; Ben create simulation harness for burst scenarios; Tom add proto metrics.
- Phase 1 (server-side, 4w): implement credit buckets, local enforcement, basic admission control, unit tests.
- Phase 2 (drain protocol, 3w): implement lease API, migration handoff, runtime flags for migrateable sessions.
- Phase 3 (canary + metrics, 2w): small canary in Dedicated, observe metrics + rollback plan.
- Phase 4 (rollout): staged rollout to more pools after 2-week observation.

Action items (owners + due dates):
- Rajat: prototype CU estimator (token vs GPU). Due 2025-02-28.
- Ben: simulate priority queue + burst behavior; produce brief. Due 2025-03-07.
- Priya: safety bounds for streaming sessions and SRE runbook updates. Due 2025-02-24.
- Tom: add proto metrics and sampling traces for lease handshakes. Due 2025-02-25.
- Marta: coordinate billing sync with Finance & Product; raise potential invoice impacts. Due 2025-03-03.
- Aisha: write RFC draft incorporating decisions + diagrams. Due 2025-02-23.

Notes / loose thoughts captured in meeting:
- Consider using predicted CU consumption from model metadata (kv cache hits reduce CU) — could reduce false negatives for credits.
- Warm-slot pool needs right-sizing: too many warm slots = wasted capacity, too few = migration failures. Simulation will help.
- For Hosted tenants, prefer transparent degraded model variant rather than queueing to avoid user-visible 429s. For Dedicated, allow queueing if tenant agreed.
- Leases need idempotency keys; plan to extend existing session id scheme.

Next steps:
- Owners start spikes and sync weekly in the serving-runtime triage (Thursday standup).
- Aisha to assemble initial RFC and share in #eng-arch for review before next architecture review (target 2025-02-26).

Appendix: quick sketches (informal) kept in CONFL-1132 — includes sequence diagrams for lease flow and credits lifecycle. Also see code PR proposer: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1123

Meeting adjourned 60m.

Inline shorthand used in notes: CU = compute units, SLO = service-level objective, QPS = queries per second, SRE = site reliability engineering
